title: Cypress Hill Embrace Latin Roots on First All-Spanish Album ‘Dios Bendiga’: ‘It’s a Prayer for the Culture’
summary: The legendary hip-hop group talk about making the LP, feat. Trueno, Alemán and more, and why now was the right time to do it.
contentText:
Some groups left an indelible mark on hip-hop history, and Cypress Hill  is without a doubt one of them. Since the early ’90s, B-Real, Sen Dog, DJ Muggs and later Eric Bobo became key figures in a scene that captured the harsh social reality of California and Los Angeles, blending innovative sounds with a Latino identity that has always been central to what they do.

That connection to their roots was cemented in 1999 with  Los Grandes Éxitos en Español , a project that brought together some of the group’s most iconic songs adapted into Spanish and ultimately became a cult classic among Latino audiences. Tracks like “Yo Quiero Fumar” and “Loco en el Coco” made it clear that the Mexican and Cuban roots of several of its members were never a side note, but a fundamental part of the band’s identity.

Now, nearly three decades later, Cypress Hill is deepening that connection with the release of  Dios Bendiga , the first album of entirely original Spanish-language material in its career. It’s a project arriving at a time when Latin rap is seeing unprecedented global growth, and one that aims to reclaim the cultural heritage that has been with the group since day one.

“ Dios Bendiga  is more than just a collection of songs; it’s a prayer for the culture. This album serves as a powerful reminder that our heritage isn’t a trend, but a divine legacy and a global future. We’re living through a historic era for Latin rap, and with this project we wanted to bring a sound that honors our history and resilience,” B-Real tells  Billboard Argentina .

And when it comes to Latin rap, Trueno was an inevitable choice. After linking up on “F*ck El Police Remix” in 2023, the group reunited with the Argentine artist on “Saca la Bolsita,” a collaboration that adds a local flavor to the new project. “Trueno is a student of hip-hop — he’s someone who’s great to work with,” Sen Dog says.

Released Friday (July 24), the album will be presented live in Buenos Aires on Nov. 8 at Estadio Malvinas Argentinas, a show with which Cypress aims to further strengthen its relationship with the South American country, which the group has been visiting since 1996.

The group’s influence, however, goes far beyond its connection to Latin culture. Over the course of its career, Cypress Hill placed seven songs on the  Billboard Hot 100  and reached one of its biggest milestones with “Insane in the Brain,” which hit No. 19 in 1993 and went on to become one of the most recognizable rap anthems of the ’90s. That same year,  Black Sunday  debuted at No. 1 on the Billboard 200 , cementing the quartet as one of the era’s most innovative and successful acts.

With more than three decades of career behind them, millions of records sold, and a legacy that has transcended generations, Cypress Hill also helped open the door for Latino artists to carve out a place within the U.S. hip-hop scene. Their blend of West Coast sounds, psychedelic influences, and a cultural identity embraced with pride ultimately became a reference point for artists now leading the global expansion of Spanish-language rap.

In that context,  Dios Bendiga  doesn’t come across as a mere curiosity within the group’s discography, but as a new statement of purpose. It’s an album that connects the past with the present and finds Cypress Hill embracing, more than ever, the language and culture that have always been part of its story.

How did the process of making an album entirely in Spanish come about?

Eric Bobo:  I think it all came from the way things started coming together in the studio — how everything flowed and ultimately clicked into place. At first, we didn’t really know exactly how we were going to approach the process. But as we moved forward, it felt like everything was happening in a very natural way.

It was as if the music wasn’t just flowing through us, but coming from something bigger. We felt a presence, something positive. For us, it was like saying, “God is with us.” From that feeling, we started developing that whole theme. On top of that, we knew it was something very close to the hearts of a lot of people in Latin America, so the concept ended up making even more sense.

How long did it take you to put everything together?

Bobo:  Honestly, it didn’t take as long as you might think. The process started last November. We finished our parts in about a month. That was surprising, because we were doing something completely different for Cypress Hill: a fully Spanish-language album, creating new music and bringing together all the pieces it needed. You’d think a project like that would take a lot longer, but everything flowed very naturally and it ended up coming together that way.

Why did you choose “Wacha Trucha” and “Campeones” as the preview singles from this album?

B-Real:  We felt that “Wacha Trucha” was a very important song for the moment we’re living in — especially because of everything that was happening with ICE and the different situations unfolding in the United States. It was kind of an alert song, a message to stay aware. But it also had a very signature Cypress Hill vibe. It reminded us of the energy of “We Ain’t Goin’ Out Like That.” We thought it was the perfect introduction to the album because that’s exactly the kind of sound a lot of people expect from us. We’ve always been a band that takes risks. We like stepping outside the box and trying different things.

Sen Dog:  With “Campeones,” we wanted to show our versatility. We wanted to prove that we could also bring a festive vibe, something closer to the Latin spirit. That’s why we chose those songs: first to show the strength, and then to show that we also know how to make music to celebrate and have a good time — not just aggressive or confrontational songs.

Do you feel like this was a return to your Latin roots?

Sen Dog:  Totally. It was a way of reconnecting with who we are, with our Latin identity and with the way we grew up in Los Angeles. We were always surrounded by the Spanish language, the slang, and that whole culture. I remember when we made  Los Grandes Éxitos , which was basically Spanish versions of Cypress Hill songs. That album had a special energy.

Honestly, I like the feeling this new album gives off even more, because everything here is original. These are new songs, new concepts. We’re not relying on anything we did in the past for this project to be embraced by the fans. Musically, it reflects much better what young Latinos around the world are doing today. I think we really captured that well. And like Eric was saying, once we got started, it was just: “Alright, let’s make an album.” Every day was the same — go to the studio, spend the day together, record songs, and come back the next day to do it all again. There were no pauses or breaks between sessions. Everyone did their part, and everything came together really well.

I remember one day walking into the studio and seeing a whiteboard with the song titles on it. At the very top it said  Dios Bendiga . In that moment I thought, “I like the way that sounds.” I don’t know exactly who came up with it, but as soon as I saw it, it felt perfect. And I know my mother would have been very happy to know we made this album.

As the lead voice, what did it mean to you, B-Real?

B-Real:  It was something we had been planning for a very long time. Sometimes your own career gets in the way of your plans. Constant touring and other albums kept taking up our time, and we never fully committed to the idea. But this time we had a serious conversation, and when the opportunity came up, we said, “If we’re going to make this album, we have to really do it.” We cleared our schedules and made sure we had no shows for about four or five months, which is pretty unusual for us because we’re normally performing all the time.
